claims.text: Terracotta means 'baked earth', and it has been used for decorative art works and for building construction since ancient times.

quotes.quote: Terracotta means 'baked earth' and it has been used to produce decorative art works as well as construction works since ancient times.
Terracotta is a ceramic material that has been used for building construction and decorative arts since ancient times in cultures around the world.

claims.text: Terracotta is made from natural clay, which gives it a characteristic reddish-brown colour.

quotes.quote: Literally translating to 'baked earth', it is made from natural clay, which gives it a characteristic reddish-brown color.

claims.text: The term ceramic refers to high-fired, glazed, vitrified wares, while pottery refers to low-fired, unvitrified objects and cooking or storage vessels.

quotes.quote: While the term ceramic is used to refer to high-fired, glazed, vitrified tableware, art objects and structural clay products; the term pottery is used to refer to low-fired, unvitrified objects and/or cooking and storage vessels.

claims.text: The word ceramic derives from the Greek keramos, which means burned material or earthenware.

quotes.quote: The term ceramic is derived from the Greek word keramos which means "burned material" or "earthenware".

claims.text: Pottery was the first synthetic material made by humans, and recorded use of clay in potting goes back eight to ten thousand years in different parts of the world.

quotes.quote: However, recorded usage of clay in potting varies between eight to ten thousand years in different parts of the world. Pottery was the first synthetic material that was created by man.

claims.text: Ceramics are made of three basic raw materials: clay, non-plastic inclusions, and water that is lost during drying and firing.

quotes.quote: Ceramics are composed of three basic raw materials: (a) clay, a sticky, fine-grained sediment that attains plasticity when wet
(b) non-plastic inclusions, mineral or organic inclusions found naturally in clays or deliberately added to alter the plasticity of the clay as desired
(c) water, added to the clays and inclusions to make them plastic and workable and that is lost during drying and firing.

claims.text: Votive terracotta in India is made by members of the Hindu potter caste, while its customer is often a member of a tribal community.

quotes.quote: Although votive terracotta is made by members of the Hindu potter caste, the customer is often a member of the Tribal community.

claims.text: Terracotta figures in India have a ritual aspect, with many terracotta figures of deities used on auspicious occasions.

quotes.quote: Terracotta figures also have a ritualistic aspect associated with it. This becomes evident from the fact that many terracotta figures of deities are used in a number of auspicious occasions.

claims.text: The Victoria and Albert Museum describes the Bankura clay horse as the most well-known type of ritual pottery from India.

quotes.quote: The most well-known type of ritual pottery from India is the Bankura clay horse

claims.text: The Kumhars take their name from the Sanskrit kumbhakar, meaning earthen pot-maker, and some Hindu kumhars call themselves Prajapati.

quotes.quote: The Kumhars obtain their name from the Sanskrit word kumbhakar, meaning earthen pot-maker. Some Hindu kumhars fondly call themselves Prajapati, after the lord who created the universe

claims.text: The terracotta artisans of Molela belong to the Kumhar, or potter, caste.

quotes.quote: Molela's terracotta artisans belong to the Kumhar ('potter') caste
there are about 40 families from the Kumhar caste producing terracotta sculptures

claims.text: At Sadum in Chittoor district the terracotta craftsmen belong to the Kummari community, the men normally throwing on the wheel and the women decorating.

quotes.quote: Sadum is a small village located 65km away from Tirupati in Chitoor district in Andhra Pradesh.
The craftsmen belong to Kummari community. In Sadum, the men are normally engaged in making the clay objects on potter's wheel, wherein the women folk perform the decoration part.

claims.text: Longpi pottery of Ukhrul district, Manipur, is traditionally made by men of the Tangkhul Naga community, though women are not barred from it.

quotes.quote: Longpi pottery is an indigenous craft practised in the district of Ukhrul, Manipur in Northeast India.
the craft is traditionally a domain of the men of the Tangkhul Naga community, although women are not prohibited from practising it.
it is the men at Longpi that make pots. However, women are not barred completely from making pots and do partake in this activity.

claims.text: An IIM Bangalore fellow found many families in Khowai district in pottery, with the Karmakar community potting for generations on ancestral knowledge.

quotes.quote: Many families in the Khowai district depend on and participate in pottery-related activities.
The MGN Fellow found out that there is one community (Karmakar) involved in pottery activities for generations and use knowledge gained from their ancestors to pursue their craft.

claims.text: Rajwar clay art, a decorative relief clay art, originated in Puhputra village in Chhattisgarh and was popularised by Sonabai Rajwar.

quotes.quote: A form of decorative relief clay art, Rajwar clay art originated in the Puhputra village in Chhattisgarh and was popularised by Sonabai Rajwar.

claims.text: Rajwar clay art is made mainly of bamboo and clay, with geometric shapes and nature motifs, by women adorning the walls and doors of their homes.

quotes.quote: Created primarily with bamboo and clay, the art form showcases several geometric shapes and motifs inspired by nature and is practised within homes by women who use it to adorn walls and doors.

claims.text: Rajwar clay art traditionally has three aspects: lepai, jhinjhari kala or jaali work, and pakha lekha or relief work.

quotes.quote: Traditionally, Rajwar clay art has three aspects - lepai, jhinjhari kala (jaali work) and pakha lekha (relief work).

claims.text: The earliest ceramics of the subcontinent, from Period IB at Mehrgarh in Baluchistan, are handmade, buff, chaff-tempered and soft.

quotes.quote: The earliest ceramics recovered from Period I B of Mehrgarh in Baluchistan are handmade, buff, chaff tempered and soft in texture.
The first ceramics of Period IB of Mehrgarh were soft, buff, chaff tempered and handmade.

claims.text: At Mehrgarh, Period IIA pottery shows slab forming, while Period IIB pottery was wheel-turned and shaped by the paddle and anvil method.

quotes.quote: Pottery from the assemblage associated with Mehrgarh II A show clear signs of forming from slabbing, while those from Period II B indicate that the pottery was wheel turned and formed using paddle and anvil method.

claims.text: Indus Valley Civilization pottery is remarkably sophisticated, with a red surface often painted with various motifs and designs.

quotes.quote: The Indus Valley Civilization is characterised by a remarkable sophistication in the production of pottery consisting of red coloured surface often painted with various motifs and designs.

claims.text: Distinctive wheel-made red pottery painted with black motifs, documented at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, became a marker for identifying sites discovered later as Indus settlements.

quotes.quote: As the first and largest cities of the civilisation to be excavated, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro came to define it
The features documented there - a distinctive wheel-made red pottery painted with black motifs
became the markers by which sites discovered later across the whole region were identified as IVC settlements

claims.text: Classical Harappan pottery is made of very well refined clay, well baked and mostly thrown on the wheel, and gives a metallic sound when struck.

quotes.quote: The ceramics of this era, popularly known as "Classical Harappan Pottery" is made of very well refined clay. It is well baked, mostly thrown on wheel, gives a metallic sound when struck.

claims.text: Painted pottery made up less than 10% of Indus pottery, the rest being unpainted and used for everyday purposes.

quotes.quote: The painted pottery of the Indus Civilization constituted <10% while the remaining ones were unpainted and used for most mundane and day to day use.

claims.text: Classical Harappan pottery is mostly reddish pink or buff, painted in contrasting black on red or dark brown on buff.

quotes.quote: Its colour is mostly reddish pink and buff (which is smaller in quantity).
For painting, a contrasting colour preferably black on red and dark brown on buff are often used.

claims.text: Indus slender jars and large goblets were built by coiling fine clay and then smoothed and finished on a wheel with burnishing tools.

quotes.quote: Some of the pottery specimen like slender jars and large goblets were manufactured using a coiling technique.

The coils of fine clay were prepared and placed one above the other, creating a rough form and shape and then the exterior surface smoothened and finished on a wheel using burnishing tools like leather, smooth pebbles, and also long chert blades.

claims.text: Ethnographic parallels suggest that large Indus storage jars were partly wheel-made and finished by hand because of their massive size.

quotes.quote: It has been observed through ethnographic parallels that large storage jars were partly wheelmade and finished by hand because of its massive size.

claims.text: Indus potters applied red ochre, an iron oxide, as a slip on leather-hard pots, and it turned bright red when heated in a kiln.

quotes.quote: While the pottery is in leather hard condition, burnishing and polishing of the surface takes place and then application of a chosen shade of red ochre (iron oxide), a naturally occurring mineral is applied
The slip applied over the pottery during leather hard condition or slightly dried condition turns bright red, the typical characteristic colour of Indus Civilization pottery, upon heating in a kiln.

claims.text: Black designs on Indus pottery were painted with a mixture of dark red-brown iron oxide and black manganese over the red ochre base.

quotes.quote: over which a different ochre shade (mixture of dark red-brown iron oxide and black manganese) is used to create the black coloured designs

claims.text: Mound E, one of the oldest mounds at Harappa, has pottery kilns alongside workshops for agate, shell and copper goods.

quotes.quote: lies Mound E, one of Harappa's oldest mounds, with pottery kilns, workshops for agate, shell and copper goods

claims.text: Harappa, an archaeological site in Punjab province of Pakistan, is the type-site of the Indus Valley Civilisation, which flourished between roughly 2600 and 1900 BCE.

quotes.quote: An archaeological site in the Punjab province of Pakistan, Harappa hosts evidence of one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, which flourished between roughly 2600 and 1900 BCE.
As the first Indus site to be excavated, Harappa is considered the archaeological type-site for the civilisation

claims.text: The most common kiln found at Indus Valley sites is the updraft type, and the best-preserved one was recently found at Khirsara in Gujarat.

quotes.quote: The most common type of kiln found in the Indus Valley sites is the updraft variety. The most elaborate and well preserved one has been recently at Khirsara (Gujarat).

claims.text: A Mature Harappan updraft kiln took fuel through a channel into an underground chamber, whose heat rose through vents in a platform under the stacked pots.

quotes.quote: The updraft kiln of the Mature Harappan period consist of a circular pit, one end emanating in the form of a huge channel to add fuel into the underground chamber, which is topped by a platform consisting of a series of fire vents, that heated the pottery assemblage stacked over it.
the heat generated gradually reaches the semi-circular chamber through the vents provided on the platform.

claims.text: Broken potsherds partly covered the platform vents of Harappan updraft kilns so that excessive direct heat would not damage and break the pottery.

quotes.quote: The vents on the platform were partly covered by broken potsherds so that heat does not directly reach the pottery, which could have damaged and broken them due to excessive heat.

claims.text: The temperature of a Harappan updraft kiln can be gauged by the colour of fumes from its vent, which turn from smoky through red and orange to bluish and transparent.

quotes.quote: The temperature can be guaged by the colour of the fumes coming out of this vent.

The initial fume coming out of these vent will be smoky, then turns into red, orange, bright orange and once the temperature reaches well above 700 - 8000 C, the colour becomes bluish and transparent.

claims.text: Harappan faience paste was made either from powdered quartz with flux and colourant or from a frit of partly melted quartz powder and colourant.

quotes.quote: In the first process, powdered quartz mixed with flux and colourant is used to produce a faience paste and in the second process, quartz powder is partly melted mixed with a colourant to produce a frit.

claims.text: The earliest recorded faience object of the Harappan civilisation is datable to 3300 BCE.

quotes.quote: The earliest recorded faience object is from Harappan datable to 3300 BCE.

claims.text: Indus terracotta animal figurines were handmade of fine fired clay mixed with sand, shell fragments, mica particles and vegetable material.

quotes.quote: These figurines are understood to have been handmade using fine fired clay, or terracotta, mixed with sand, shell fragments, mica particles and vegetable material.

claims.text: Evidence suggests that some early Indus figurines, largely from Mehrgarh and Nausharo in Balochistan, date as far back as 7000 BCE.

quotes.quote: Evidence suggests that some early Indus figurines, that were largely excavated from the Mehrgarh and Nausharo sites in the Balochistan province of present-day Pakistan, date as far back as 7000 BCE, prior to the Early Harappan Phase.

claims.text: Nearly three-quarters of Indus terracotta animal figurines represent cattle, often humped bulls and buffaloes.

quotes.quote: Nearly three-quarters of the animal figurines represent cattle, often humped bulls and buffaloes.

claims.text: Indus female terracotta figurines were made by potters, bought by individuals for rituals, and later discarded for children to use as toys.

quotes.quote: These female figurines are also identified by some scholars as mother goddess and could have been used as a ritualistic symbol.
These figurines were manufactured by potters and purchased by individuals for conducting rituals and later discarded to be used by children as toys.

claims.text: Black and Red Ware spans the Neolithic to the Early Historic Period and spread across most of the Indian subcontinent.

quotes.quote: Black and Red Ware is significant for its chronological span - from the Neolithic Period to the Early Historic Period - as well as its geographical spread across most of the subcontinent.

claims.text: Black and Red Ware was first excavated and described by Mortimer Wheeler in 1947, and was at first called Satavahana Ware.

quotes.quote: Black and Red Ware was first excavated and described by Mortimer Wheeler in 1947 and was initially called Satavahana Ware.

claims.text: In western India, Black and Red Ware is associated with the Harappan culture at sites such as Lothal, Somnath and Bet Dwarka.

quotes.quote: In Western India, Black and Red Ware pottery is associated with the Harappan culture at sites such as Lothal, Somnath (Prabhas Patan) and Bet Dwarka.

claims.text: Most Black and Red Ware objects have a red exterior surface and a black interior surface.

quotes.quote: While both colours may appear on the same surface, most objects typically have a red exterior surface and a black interior surface.

claims.text: Black and Red Ware's colours may have come from inverted firing, the outer surface oxidising to red while the vegetal-filled inside was reduced to black.

quotes.quote: The colour of the surfaces may have been achieved using the inverted firing technique, in which the pot is positioned upside-down in a kiln, with the interior filled with vegetal matter.
When fired, the outer surface is oxidised, resulting in the red colour, while the inner surface is subject to reduction conditions, turning it black.

claims.text: Black and Red Ware's two-coloured surfaces are said to result from inverted firing or from baking vessels mouth to mouth, cutting oxygen to the interiors.

quotes.quote: the contrasting colour effect on both the surfaces are said to be either the result of inverted firing or by keeping the vessels mouth to mouth while baking, thereby arresting the supply of oxygen to the interiors.

claims.text: Some scholars have suggested that a double-firing technique may have produced the red and black surfaces of Black and Red Ware.

quotes.quote: Some scholars have suggested that a double-firing technique may have been used to achieve the same result.

claims.text: Similar pottery from ancient Egypt of the fourth millennium BCE has led to speculation that the black and red firing technique may have originated there.

quotes.quote: The discovery of a similar kind of pottery in ancient Egypt, dated to the fourth millennium BCE, has led to speculation that the technique may have originated there.

claims.text: Northern Black Polished Ware, an Iron Age pottery type with glossy surfaces, is dated to between 700 BCE and 200 BCE.

quotes.quote: Dated to between 700 BCE and 200 BCE, during the Early Historic Period in the Indian subcontinent, Northern Black Polished Ware is an Iron Age pottery type characterised by glossy surfaces.

claims.text: Northern Black Polished Ware is made of fine levigated clay turned on a fast wheel, with a burnished glossy slip ranging from jet black to steel blue.

quotes.quote: Northern Black Polished Ware is made of fine levigated clay turned on a fast wheel, and features a burnished, glossy slip on the exterior and interior surfaces that can range from jet black to grey to steel blue in colour.

claims.text: How Northern Black Polished Ware's glossy finish was achieved remains debated; explanations include an iron compound and firing in reduction conditions.

quotes.quote: How the glossy finish was achieved remains debated and has been ascribed to the use of an iron compound and the firing of pots in reduction conditions, with the application of oil or plant matter immediately after firing or a clay solution made of fine particles.

claims.text: Damaged Northern Black Polished Ware vessels were repaired with copper wire or riveting, a sign of the value placed on the ware.

quotes.quote: The value of this ware can be gauged by the fact that damaged utensils were repaired with copper wire or riveting

claims.text: Because Northern Black Polished Ware formed only around 5 percent of its sites' pottery, it has been speculated to have been a luxury item.

quotes.quote: Northern Black Polished Ware also comprised only a small percentage of the ceramic assemblage at sites where it was found - in this instance, around 5 percent
This has led to the speculation that Northern Black Polished Ware would have been a luxury item.

claims.text: Scholars suggest that Painted Grey Ware may have been a luxury category of objects, likely used by wealthy groups.

quotes.quote: The size and form of the objects and the relatively small yield have led scholars to suggest that Painted Grey Ware pottery may have been a luxury category of objects likely used by wealthy groups.

claims.text: Painted Grey Ware, largely dated to 1100-400 BCE, is a post-Harappan culture of the Indo-Gangetic plain named after its finely made painted grey pottery.

quotes.quote: Largely dated to 1100-400 BCE, with some sites dated to 1400 BCE, the Painted Grey Ware Culture was a post-Harappan material culture found primarily in the Indo-Gangetic plain, named after the finely made painted grey pottery found in the region.

claims.text: Painted Grey Ware was thrown on a fast wheel to egg-shell thickness, turned again when hard to trim it, and finished with black slip or painted designs.

quotes.quote: The objects were made on a fast wheel and shaped to an egg-shell thickness. Once hard, they were again turned on the wheel to trim and smooth the surface and finished with a thick black slip or painted with black and brown designs.

claims.text: Painted Grey Ware made up only 3-10% of the pottery recovered within its own assemblages.

quotes.quote: Although it lends its name to the culture, Painted Grey Ware pottery comprised only 3-10% of the pottery artefacts recovered within its assemblage and was found with other types such as Plain Grey Ware, Black and Red Ware and Black Slip Ware.

claims.text: Ochre Coloured Pottery of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab is ill-fired, wheel-made red ware with a thick red slip, often heavily weathered.

quotes.quote: the Ochre Coloured Pottery Culture (OCP Culture) is a cultural sequence defined by its characteristic ill-fired, wheel-made ceramics with a fine or medium fabric and a thick red slip.
Within the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, the Localization Era is characterized by the appearance of Ochre Coloured Pottery. It is illfired, red in colour and heavily weathered with the slip peeling off.

claims.text: Terracottas from Chandraketugarh in North 24 Parganas, dated third century BCE to third century CE, are the most numerous and varied of their period from any single region.

quotes.quote: Dated to between the third century BCE and the third century CE, the terracotta objects uncovered from Chandraketugarh in North 24 Parganas district, West Bengal form some of the most important archaeological discoveries related to the arts of ancient India.
These objects constitute the greatest number and variety of specimens from this time period found from any single region in the Indian subcontinent.

claims.text: Chandraketugarh terracottas are known for their sophistication and unique visual style, often highly embellished with distinctive surface stippling.

quotes.quote: Known for their sophistication and unique visual style, the Chandraketugarh terracottas are often highly embellished with a distinctive surface stippling.

claims.text: Stratigraphic dating of Chandraketugarh's terracottas is unreliable because the deltaic soil, fed by the Ganga and Brahmaputra, has often flooded and shifted.

quotes.quote: Stratigraphic dating is not sufficiently reliable here because the deltaic soil of the region, fed by the rivers Ganga and Brahmaputra, has undergone frequent flooding and shifting since ancient times.

claims.text: By the end of the 16th century CE, a new Bengali style of temple art became prominent as an artistic Hindu expression, an ORF commentary notes.

quotes.quote: by the end of the 16th century CE, a new Bengali style of temple art became prominent that established itself as an artistic Hindu expression.

claims.text: The terracotta temples of Bankura are mostly Radha-Krishna temples that drew inspiration from Vaishnavism.

quotes.quote: The terracotta temples in Bankura are mostly Radha-Krishna temples which drew inspiration from Vaishnavism.

claims.text: Locals told an ORF author that Bankura terracotta once had separate clay collectors and sievers, detailing artisans and traders, roles no longer distinct.

quotes.quote: According to the locals, previously, the process of terracotta production in Bankura included three major classes of workers: the clay collectors and seivers, who would give a fine texture to the clay; the artisans who would add the intricate details, and finally the market traders.
There is no specific class of labour anymore for each of these three roles.

claims.text: The V&A records Bankura clay horses, elephants and tigers bought by villagers as offerings to the forest gods against wild animals, a ritual offering no longer widespread.

quotes.quote: The most well-known type of ritual pottery from India is the Bankura clay horse
which along with other animal forms like elephants and tigers are bought by villagers, as offerings to the forest gods for protection against wild animals.
and this type of ritual offering is no longer widespread

claims.text: The V&A records that Bankura's once dense forests and wild animals have practically disappeared, and the ritual offering of clay animals is no longer widespread.

quotes.quote: However, the once dense forests and numerous wild animals of Bankura have practically disappeared, and this type of ritual offering is no longer widespread.

claims.text: Bihar and Bankura district both have a vivid tradition of terracotta elephants, lions and horses, with or without riders, as ritual figures.

quotes.quote: Both Bihar and Bankura district have a vivid tradition of making figures of elephant, lion and horses, with or without a rider as ritual figures.

claims.text: Terracotta horses and horse riders were offered as votive objects and placed at wayside altars and shrines.

quotes.quote: Horse and horse riders are also offered as votive objects. These were placed at wayside altars and shrines.

claims.text: The Bankura horse tradition, patronised by the Malla dynasty of Bishnupur, is related to the deity Dharmaraja, a form of the sun god.

quotes.quote: This craft tradition, patronized by the Malla dynasty of Bishnupur, got a Geographical Indication tag for West Bengal.
This craft is related to the Dharmaraja deity, a form of the sun god.

claims.text: A Panchmura potter told an ORF author that the Bankura horse arose as an offering to deities and even on the tombs of Muslim saints.

quotes.quote: The trademark Bankura horse (uniquely styled terracotta horse made in Bankura) came into existence because people would offer them as a mark of devotion to different deities and even on the tombs of Muslim saints.

claims.text: The Bankura district page says the long-necked terracotta horse comes in seven separate body parts, such as a hollow neck, legs, face, ears and tail, which are assembled.

quotes.quote: You will see that the horse comes in seven separated body parts like a hollow long neck, four legs, face, ears, tail etc. You have to assemble those parts to get a horse like structure.

claims.text: A painted Bankura horse of c.1944 in the V&A is hollow and partly hand-modelled, with applied pellet eyes and openings at the mouth, hooves and rear.

quotes.quote: Painted terracotta horse, Bankura district, India, c.1944
Partially hand-modelled figure of a horse with some incised details, such as the mane. Pellets have been applied for the eyes. The figure is hollow and has openings in the mouth, hooves and rear.

claims.text: The V&A records that the Bankura clay horse was adopted as the motif of the Central Cottage Industries Emporium, a government handicrafts marketing body.

quotes.quote: Today the clay horse is a popular art object in its own right and has been adopted as the motif for the Central Cottage Industries Emporium, the central marketing body of Indian handicrafts set up by the Government of India.

claims.text: The Bankura horse is the official crest motif of the All India Handicrafts Board.

quotes.quote: The Bankura horse is the official crest-motif of the 'All India Handicrafts Board'.
Enhance the grace of your drawing room with the long-necked Terracotta Horse which is the logo of All India Handicrafts.

claims.text: A DC(H) project report calls the Ayanaar horse of Tamil Nadu the largest terracotta sculpture ever made, built by coiling and beating like vessels.

quotes.quote: For instance the impressive Ayanaar horse from Tamil nadu represents the largest terracotta sculpture ever made and is constructed from coiling and beating, the same techniques used for making vessels.

claims.text: In West Bengal the snake goddess Manasa is worshipped through a terracotta tree shrine built from multiple thrown and modelled parts.

quotes.quote: In West Bengal, the snake goddess Manasa is worshipped through a terracotta tree shrine constructed from multiple thrown and modelled parts.

claims.text: Relief plaques of tribal deities made in Rajasthan and the horses and tigers recorded in Gujarat are made for tribal clientele.

quotes.quote: The relief plaques depicting images of Tribal deities are made in Rajasthan and the varied styles of horses and tigers recorded in Gujrat are also made for Tribal clientele.

claims.text: Madhya Pradesh's terracotta includes highly embellished elephants offered in forest shrines, as well as women's wall decoration.

quotes.quote: Madhya Pradesh is represented by the highly embellished elephants offered in forest shrines and also by women's wall decoration.

claims.text: Communities of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, particularly the Bhil, and the Gujjar have bought Molela plaques as votives, accompanied by their priests.

quotes.quote: Historically various communities of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat - particularly the Bhil - as well as the Gujjar of northwest India, have purchased Molela plaques as votives.
These are mostly bought by the Bhil, Gujjar and Gajirat communities who arrive here accompanied by their priests in order to buy new votive images of their deities.

claims.text: Several temples in southern Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh replace their idols every year and come to Molela for terracotta figurines.

quotes.quote: Several temples in Southern Rajasthan and also in Madhya Pradesh replace the idols every year, and visit Molela for the beautiful terracotta figurines that are created here.

claims.text: Molela plaques show Hindu deities such as Chamunda, Kali, Durga and Ganesha, regional divinities like Nagadeva, and folk heroes such as Devnarayan and Tejaji.

quotes.quote: The deities on the plaques range from widely worshipped Hindu deities, such as Chamunda, Kali, Durga, and Ganesha, to more regional cult divinities, such as Nagadeva.
folk heroes from local legends also feature prominently, such as Devnarayan, Tejaji, Pabuji, Gora Bhairav, Kala Bhairav, and Panchmukhi.

claims.text: Hereditary potters at Molela have made hand-moulded, hollow-relief terracotta plaques since perhaps the seventeenth century.

quotes.quote: Terracotta plaques with hand-moulded, hollow relief imagery have been made by hereditary potters in Molela, a village in Rajasthan in northwestern India, since perhaps the seventeenth century.

claims.text: Invest India's ODOP team states that the Molela clay-work art form dates back over 5000 years.

quotes.quote: This Molela Clay-Work artform dates back to over 5000 years.

claims.text: Khurja, in present-day Uttar Pradesh, is a historic centre of ceramic production said to have been established in the 14th century.

quotes.quote: It was made by the potter Abdul Majid in Khurja, a historic centre of ceramic production said to have been established in the 14th century and still renowned for its ceramic industry.
The name of the town in present-day Uttar Pradesh means 'waste land'.

claims.text: Incredible India says potters from Multan are believed to have started Khurja pottery, and a number of artisans call themselves Multani Kumhars.

quotes.quote: It is believed that potters from Multan came to the town of Khurja and started practicing pottery. In fact, a number of artisans often call themselves 'Multani Kumhars' hinting at the origin of the craft.

claims.text: According to George Watt in 1903, Khurja had originally produced pottery with slip decoration raised in slight relief, white and blue on an orange-brown or claret ground.

quotes.quote: According to Sir George Watt in the official catalogue of the Delhi Exhibition of 1902-1903, Indian Art at Delhi, 1903, Khurja had originally produced pottery in a style all of its own
with decoration raised in slight relief by the use of slips in floral patterns picked out in white and blue against a warm orange brown or pale claret coloured field

claims.text: By the time of the Delhi Exhibition, George Watt lamented that Khurja's distinctive style had vanished and its wares imitated those of Multan.

quotes.quote: By the time of the Delhi Exhibition Watt laments that the disctinctive style of Khurja had vanished and that their wares imitated those made at Multan

claims.text: The origin of Nizamabad black pottery can be traced back to the period of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb.

quotes.quote: The origin of this art can be traced back to the period of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb.

claims.text: Chunar glaze pottery of Uttar Pradesh traces its origin to the 17th century, when Mughal rulers patronised the art form.

quotes.quote: The origin of this craft can be traced back to the 17th century, when Mughal rulers patronized this artform.
For centuries the craft of Chunar Glaze Pottery has formed an integral part of a rich cultural heritage of Uttar Pradesh.

claims.text: Villianur terracotta is traced back to the Chola period of the 9th to 13th centuries, but flourished only in the 18th and 19th centuries under French rule.

quotes.quote: The origin of Villianur Terracotta can be traced back to the Chola period (9th to 13th centuries), when the region was under the influence of the Chola dynasty. The art form, however flourished only during the 18th and 19th centuries under the French colonial rule.

claims.text: Longpi was a meeting place of villages, including Naga ones, and its potters historically traded their pots in exchange for salt.

quotes.quote: Historically, the Longpi region formed a meeting place for several villages, including those of neighbouring Nagaland, and the craftspeople traded the pottery in exchange for salt.
Men carrying ham in traditional baskets supplied the ham to fellow Nagas, who bought it in exchange of salt.

claims.text: Ursula Graham Bower noted in her journal that no wheel was used at Longpi, where the clay was rolled up round a bamboo to shape it.

quotes.quote: As Ursula Graham Bower noted in her journal,
No wheel was used. The clay was rolled up round a bamboo to bring it to the right shape

claims.text: Clay is a naturally occurring, fine-grained material that is generally plastic at appropriate water contents and hardens when dried or fired.

quotes.quote: naturally occurring material composed primarily of fine-grained materials, including crystalline and amorphous oxides and hydroxides of various metals, which are generally plastic at appropriate water contents and will harden when dried or fired
The term clay is usually defined as fine-grained earthy material that becomes plastic or malleable when moistened.

claims.text: Most clay minerals are layered silicates, or phyllosilicates, and the strength of the bonds between layers influences their plasticity.

quotes.quote: Mineralogically, most clay minerals belong to the category of layered silicates or phyllosilicates. The strength of bonds between layers influence the plasticity of the different clay groups.
Clays are silicates belonging to the phyllosilicate group.

claims.text: The major clay mineral groups are kaolinite, smectite or montmorillonite, and illite.

quotes.quote: The major clay mineral groups are kaolinite, smectite or montmorillonite and illite.

claims.text: Clay minerals are built of tetrahedral and octahedral sheets arranged in layers, 1:1 layers being about 0.7 nm thick and 2:1 layers about 1 nm.

quotes.quote: Their structure consists of octahedral (O) or tetrahedral (T) sheets firmly arranged in structural layers.
the thickness of the 1:1 (T-O) layer is about 0.7 nm, and the 2:1 (T-O-T) layer is about 1 nm

claims.text: Kaolinites have a two-layered structure and larger particles than other clay minerals, and they fire to a white or yellow colour.

quotes.quote: Kaolinites have a two layered structure and their particle size is large when compared to other mineral types.
Kaolinites fire to white or yellow colour.

claims.text: Sedimentary kaolinites have good plasticity, while residual kaolinites have low plasticity and low shrinkage.

quotes.quote: While the plasticity of sedimentary kaolinites is good, residual kaolinites have low plasticity and their shrinkage is low.

claims.text: Kaolinites form through intense weathering of parent rock, mostly by acid leaching, and occur as both primary and secondary clays.

quotes.quote: Kaolinites occur as primary and secondary clays and are formed because of intense weathering of the parent rock mostly due to acid leaching and are considerably wide-spread.

claims.text: Smectites, formerly called montmorillonites, have very small particles and a three-layered structure, and are very plastic with a high shrinkage rate.

quotes.quote: Smectites, formerly known as montmorillonites
The particle size of smectites is very small and they have a three layered structure. Smectites are very plastic and have a high shrinkage rate.

claims.text: Smectites are characteristic of arid and alkaline environments and are not heavily weathered.

quotes.quote: Smectites, formerly known as montmorillonites are characteristic of arid and alkaline environments and are not heavily weathered.

claims.text: When fired, smectites take on cream, red and light brown colours, while illites fire to variable colours.

quotes.quote: When fired smectites attain cream, red and light brown colours.
On firing, illites attain variable colours.

claims.text: Illites occur mostly in marine and calcareous sediments, have a three-layered structure and small particles, and have considerably good plasticity.

quotes.quote: Illites occur mostly in marine and calcareous sediments and have a three-layered structure. They have considerably good plasticity and small particles.

claims.text: Bentonite is a rock whose dominant clay minerals are smectites formed through the weathering of volcanic glass.

quotes.quote: Bentonite is term for rock whose dominant clay minerals are smectites formed through the weathering of volcanic glass

claims.text: Bentonites are the most plastic of the common clays, while many clay raw materials are not plastic.

quotes.quote: Bentonites are the most plastic common clay. Many clay raw materials are not plastic.

claims.text: Common clays, which often contain illite and smectite mixed-layer minerals, serve ceramics in general except porcelain.

quotes.quote: Common clay Sedimentary or by weathering Often illite/smectite mixed-layer minerals General for ceramics excluding porcelain

claims.text: Fuller's earth, known as Multani Mitti, is a very fine clay whose main mineral is montmorillonite, sometimes with palygorskite or sepiolite.

quotes.quote: Fuller's earth Sedimentary, residual, or hydrothermal Montmorillonite, sometimes palygorskite, sepiolite
Multani Mitti or Fullers Earth is very fine in nature and is available in form of solid lumps.

claims.text: Large amounts of smectite in a clay may develop undesirable shrinkage and drying properties.

quotes.quote: Large amounts of smectite may develop undesirable shrinkage and drying properties.

claims.text: Plasticity is the property that lets a material be deformed under stress without rupturing and keep the new shape once the stress is removed.

quotes.quote: Plasticity was defined as a property which permits a material to be deformed under stress without rupturing and to retain the shape produced after the stress is removed

claims.text: Ball clays are highly plastic but crack when dried, bentonites can take a week to dry, and kaolins dry quickly with little shrinkage.

quotes.quote: For example, ball clays are highly plastic, but undesirable cracks are formed when they are dried. Bentonites have a high affinity for water that it can take a week to dry a specimen. Kaolins can dry in a short time and have little shrinkage.

claims.text: Non-plastic raw materials such as feldspars and quartz are not plastic with water, and partly act as fillers that reduce plasticity or shrinkage of a body.

quotes.quote: Non-plastic ceramic raw materials (containing feldspars, quartz, limestone, dolomite, magnesite, calcium phosphate and talc) when mixed with water are not plastic.
A part of the non-plastic ceramic raw materials acts as a filler for reducing of high plasticity or shrinkage of the body when drying or firing.

claims.text: To improve workability and strengthen pot walls, potters add organic inclusions like ash, husk and chaff, or inorganic ones like quartz, lime and grog.

quotes.quote: To improve the workability of the clay and add strength to the walls of the pottery, non -plastic inclusions are added to the clay. These include organic materials like ash, husks of grains, chaff as well as inorganic materials like quartz, lime and grog.

claims.text: The non-plastic inclusions make up from 20% to 50% of the total volume of a clay body, the share varying with its plasticity.

quotes.quote: The proportion of these non-plastic inclusions greatly varies with the plasticity from 20% to 50% of the total volume

claims.text: Potters also combine different clays to improve plasticity, then add water and knead the clay to remove air pockets and make it homogenous.

quotes.quote: Apart from the non-plastic inclusions potters also combine different clays to improve the plasticity and enhance the workability. Water is then added to the clay in order to make it plastic and then it is kneaded well.
The kneading or blending of the clay is done to remove the air pockets and also to make the clay homogenous

claims.text: Impurities are removed from clay by hand-picking or by pounding dried clay through a sieve, and in more recent times very fine clay is separated by levigation.

quotes.quote: Impurities are removed from clay either by hand-picking or by drying damp clays and pounding them and passing them through a sieve.
A more elaborate technique of levigation where coarse impurities settle in the bottom and the fine clay mixed with water is separated is used in more recent times for very fine clay.

claims.text: Primary clays stay at their parent rock and are coarse and non-plastic, while secondary clays are carried away by streams, rivers, glaciation, erosion and wind.

quotes.quote: Primary or residual clays are those deposits which remain in the same location as the parent rock from which they have formed.
These deposits are coarse grained and non-plastic as the clay was not transported by water.
Secondary or transported or sedimentary clays are found in deposits some distance from a probable parent source, transported by streams, rivers, glaciation, erosion and wind.

claims.text: Sedimentary clays are more common than residual clays, finer and more homogenous because they are sorted and redeposited, and richer in organic content.

quotes.quote: Sedimentary clays are more common than the residual clays and are more homogenous as well as finer in texture, for they are well-sorted and redeposited by external agencies. In comparison with the residual clays they are comparatively higher in organic content.

claims.text: Clays are products of the weathering of silicate rocks and are composed mainly of silica and alumina, the elements most resistant to weathering.

quotes.quote: Clays being the products of weathering of silicate rocks, are primarily composed of silica and alumina, the two chemical elements most resistant to weathering.

claims.text: The formation of clay is a chemical process assisted by mechanical breakdown and the separation of fine particles from coarse grains.

quotes.quote: The formation of clay is a chemical process that is assisted by mechanical breakdown and the separation of fine particles from coarse grains

claims.text: Arnold is of the opinion that potters obtain clay close to home, 1 to 6 kilometers from the manufacturing site, while temper is often brought from farther away.

quotes.quote: Arnold is of the opinion that potters obtain their raw materials from sources close to home. Clays are procured from 1 to 6 kilometers from the manufacturing site
Tempering materials are often transported from sources farther away because the quantity of temper is much lesser than the clay quantities.

claims.text: Glazes consist of silica, fluxes that lower their melting point, and metallic oxides that give colour to the surface of the pot.

quotes.quote: Glazes comprise of silica, fluxes which reduce the melting point of the glazes and metallic oxides that provide colour to the surface of the pot.

claims.text: Slipping coats the whole pot with liquid clay before firing, which changes its colour and also reduces its porosity.

quotes.quote: Slipping includes applying a uniform coat of liquid clay all over the pot before firing. This not only alters the colour but also reduces the porosity of the pot.

claims.text: Smoothing, burnishing and polishing with a stone or smoothed potsherd reduce a pot's porosity by aligning the clay particles on its surface.

quotes.quote: These techniques do not involve application of colour and uses a hard tool like a stone or a broken and smoothed potsherd in the process.
These surface finishing techniques reduce the porosity of the pot by aligning the clay particles on the surface.

claims.text: Pottery is formed in two broad ways, by hand-building or by throwing on the wheel, and Neolithic potters often used more than one hand-building method.

quotes.quote: Forming of pottery can be done in two ways, hand-building techniques and wheel-thrown techniques. There are various ways pottery can be made employing hand-building techniques and often more than one method is used in pottery making in the Neolithic.

claims.text: Coiling, the most common hand-building technique, builds a pot's walls by laying moistened clay coils one on top of another.

quotes.quote: The most common of all hand-made techniques is the coiling technique.
The walls of the pots are built by placing the coils successively one on top of the other. The coils moistened by the potter so that they adhere to each other.

claims.text: Hand-building also includes pinching for small pots, slab building for non-round shapes, and moulds of stone, broken pots, baskets or gourds.

quotes.quote: The simplest among the hand-building techniques is the pinching method
This method can be used only to make small pots and walls of the pottery are randomly uneven.
Slab building technique is employed on both small and large pots with a non-round shape.
Stones, broken pots, baskets and gourds are used as moulds.

claims.text: In the paddle and anvil method, a rounded stone anvil is held inside a leather-hard pot while a wooden paddle beats the outside.

quotes.quote: The paddle and anvil method comprises the use of a rounded stone anvil and a wooden mallet shaped paddle. The anvil is held in the interior of the pot while the exterior is beaten by the paddle.
This method is applied to pots when they are in a leather hard state

claims.text: Paddle and anvil beating thins and compacts the pot wall, increasing its strength and decreasing its porosity, and is used mostly for round-based cooking pots.

quotes.quote: This not only increases the diameter of the pot but also makes the wall of the pot thin and compact thus increasing the strength and also decreasing the porosity of the pot
Paddle and anvil technique is mostly used in producing round-based pots, mostly cooking pots.

claims.text: At Sadum, pots are thinned by beating the outside with a wooden bat called salapa while a mushroom-shaped stone, the raayi, is held inside.

quotes.quote: A mushroom shaped stone-known as Raayi locally which is used to beat the inner surface of objects like pot, vessels etc. where in the Salapa-wooden bat is used to beat the outer surface of the pot.

Some objects such as pots, bowls, and vessels are beaten with a flat wooden bat and a mushroom shaped stone which is held inside the object. This process is repeated until the required thinness is achieved.

claims.text: Longpi uses the beaten pottery common in Manipur: the potter keeps one hand inside and beats the clay from outside with a wet paddle called hamkapi.

quotes.quote: Like in the rest of the state, the common technique of beaten pottery appears at Longpi.

the potter then shapes the vessel, keeping one hand on the inside while continuously beating the clay from the outside using a wet hamkapi, a wooden or bamboo paddle with a cylindrical handle and flat head

claims.text: Longpi pottery is made of powdered black serpentine rock, lishong or leshong lung, mixed with clay, ngalung, in NID's account, or with weathered reddish-brown rock, salla nali, in Imp-art's.

quotes.quote: The village abounds in serpentine rock or lishong lung, a primary material used for making ham.
After having powdered the rock it is mixed with clay or ngalung.
Longpi pottery is made using a mixture of two materials, leshong lung (black serpentine stone) and leshon or salla nali (weathered reddish-brown rock), which are found in abundance in the area.

claims.text: Longpi sits on a vast body of serpentine rock, sometimes visible at the surface, which the villagers dig from the nearby hill of Kaphung Reim.

quotes.quote: The village sits on this vast geological material with the rock sometimes visible on the surface. The villagers procure the rock from Kaphung Reim, a nearby hill.

claims.text: Between September and March the men of Longpi dig and store the serpentine rock so that it can be used through the long monsoon months.

quotes.quote: Between the months of September and March, men at the village, busy themselves in digging the rock and preserving it so that it could be used during the long spell of monsoon months.

claims.text: Longpi pots are air-dried for four to twelve days, usually over the hearth, then fired in an open furnace or a closed kiln.

quotes.quote: The pot is then air-dried for four to twelve days, usually over the hearth inside the house, before it is fired in an open furnace or a closed kiln

claims.text: D'source records that Molela potters mix equal parts of nada, a coarse black clay with a high sand grog, and finer grey alu, adding 20% dried donkey dung.

quotes.quote: Nada, a coarse black clay with a high sand grog and Alu, a finer gray clay used for throwing. The two clays are mixed together in equal parts with the addition of 20% dried and sifted donkey dung
The clay used for Molela terracotta products is a mix of the coarse black nada clay and the finer grey alu clay

claims.text: D'source and Imp-art say the donkey dung in Molela clay disperses heat through the plaque during firing, gives it strength and lessens thermal shock.

quotes.quote: which helps to disperse the heat through the plaque, provides strength and lessons the thermal shock during firing.
The fine sifted clay is then mixed with vegetable gum, wheat or maize chaff, and donkey dung - the latter lends strength and helps disperse heat during the firing.

claims.text: Molela figures are built hollow with one hand kept underneath, which reduces weight and spreads heat evenly during firing, minimising cracking.

quotes.quote: keeping one hand under to ensure that the forms are hollow. Besides reducing the weight of the piece, this allows for even heat distribution during firing, minimising cracking.
they are hollow giving rise to lightweight pieces of art. This technique prevents formation of cracks and also uses less amount of clay.

claims.text: Imp-art places Molela's grey alu clay in the bed of the nearby Banas River and local ponds, and Incredible India has the clay dug from the Banas banks.

quotes.quote: the finer grey alu clay found in the bed of the nearby Banas River and local ponds
Molela is a supple and sticky clay, which is dug out from the banks of the river Banas.

claims.text: Molela's clay is typically collected during the monsoon, when it is most abundant.

quotes.quote: from where it is typically collected during the monsoon when it is most abundant.

claims.text: At Molela, moulding is usually done in the monsoon, when the humidity in the air helps reduce cracking in the clay.

quotes.quote: The moulding is usually done in the monsoon, when the humidity in the air helps reduce cracking in the clay.

claims.text: In Panchmura the potter's wheel stops in the holy time of Baisakh, in April and May, believed to be when Lord Shiva appears from the wheel, though many also cite heat that tires artisans and cracks pottery.

quotes.quote: The norwesters in the potters' village of Panchmura is magnificent in ways more than one.
The extremely dry atmosphere during the summer months of April-May
This period is marked by the holy time of Baisakh when the potter's wheel is stopped as it is believed that during this time Lord Shiva appears from the wheel.
Many justify it with a scientific reason that the terrible heat exhausts the artisans easily and develop cracks in the pottery items.

claims.text: Gorakhpur terracotta uses a local clay called Kabis, found in ponds only in May and June, and the pottery has a distinctive natural red colour.

quotes.quote: Made with the locally available clay called 'Kabis', found in the ponds only in the months of May and June, the Gorakhpur Terracota pottery has a distinctive natural red colour.

claims.text: At Sadum the clay comes from local ponds and is mixed with sand, isuka, and water, then stamped and crushed into a dough.

quotes.quote: The rich clay found in local ponds is very suitable for making clay idols.
Now the raw materials such as isuka-sand, matti-clay are added with water to prepare the dough. The craftsmen mix the clay by stamping and crushing for the better mixing of clay.

claims.text: In the Khemli terracotta cluster, clay is strained of coarse particles, mixed with water and donkey dung powder, left for 24 hours and kneaded.

quotes.quote: In the first phase of making, the clay is strained to rid of the coarse particles & unwanted material. Following which, an appropriate amount of water, & donkey dung powder is mixed, and left for 24 hours. Dough is made by a rigorous kneading of the wet clay.

claims.text: Nizamabad's black pottery uses a mica-rich clay, procured in the summer months and stored in houses through the year.

quotes.quote: the making of the pottery requires clay, which is procured during the summer months to be stored in the houses through the year. The clay, which is rich in mica, is meticulously molded on the potter's wheel into a desired shape and then sun dried for several days.

claims.text: Nizamabad's black colour comes from keeping the kiln airtight, an oxygen-free firing, because oxygen tends to turn clay red.

quotes.quote: The unusual black colour of the pottery is achieved by creating an oxygen free environment in the kiln. As oxygen tends to turn clay red, the potters ensure that the kilns are kept air tight during the firing process and thus clay acquires black colour.

claims.text: The etched grooves of Nizamabad pottery are filled with a silver paint described as a blend of equal amounts of lead, zinc and mercury.

quotes.quote: silver paint,which is a blend of an equal amount of lead, zinc, and mercury, is used to fill the grooves of the etched patterns.

claims.text: At Nizamabad, women etch intricate patterns on the dried clay with a fine needle.

quotes.quote: The women folk then etch intricate patterns on the dried clay with a fine needle.

claims.text: At Sadum, ware comes out red when smoke escapes through the kiln vents and black when the vents are fully covered so no smoke leaves.

quotes.quote: The objects after firing turn into two different colors such as red and black. The red color is obtained when the smoke comes out through the vents of the kiln. Where in the black color is obtained by covering the vents completely without allowing the smoke to come out.

claims.text: A firing atmosphere is oxidising when oxygen is present and reducing when very little is, and with organic matter it affects a pot's colour, porosity, shrinkage and hardness.

quotes.quote: When oxygen is present, an oxidizing atmosphere exists and when there is very little presence of oxygen a reducing atmosphere exists. The firing atmosphere along with the presence of organic matter in the clay paste affects the pot colour, porosity, shrinkage and hardness

claims.text: Oxidising firing burns off organic matter to give a light colour, while in reducing conditions carbon from the fuels is deposited on pots, leaving black or dark brown surfaces.

quotes.quote: In oxidizing conditions, the organic matter in the clay and the fuels is burnt and a light colour is achieved. In reducing conditions, carbon in the clay paste is lost and the carbon from the fuels is also deposited on the surface of the pots resulting in black or dark brown coloured surfaces.

claims.text: The final appearance of a pot's surface depends on the maximum firing temperature, the duration of the firing and the firing atmosphere.

quotes.quote: The final appearance of the surface of pottery largely depends on three aspects, the maximum temperature attained during firing, the duration of the firing process and also the firing atmosphere

claims.text: Firing at a minimum of 550°C is needed for pottery of considerable hardness and durability, and irreversible changes in clay structure begin at 500° C.

quotes.quote: A minimum of 550°C is needed to produce pottery for considerable hardness and durability.
Irreversible changes in the clay structure occur at 500° C and above.

claims.text: In sintering, clay minerals decompose and grain edges bond by ion diffusion; kaolinite restructures at 585° C and smectite at 678° C.

quotes.quote: Clay minerals start to decompose and edges of the grains bond together by ion diffusion which is known as 'sintering'. While kaolinite decomposes and restructures at 585° C, smectite attains the same at relatively high temperature of 678° C

claims.text: At 900° C clay minerals lose their structure and form new silicate minerals.

quotes.quote: At 900° C clay minerals lose their structure and form new silicate minerals.

claims.text: Ceramic sintering processes occur at temperatures higher than 800°C.

quotes.quote: Ceramic processes during sintering occur at temperatures higher than 800°C.

claims.text: Between 500° C and 600° C a pot loses some inclusions, such as carbon, sulfides, carbonates and salts, and shrinks by about 15% or more of its original mass.

quotes.quote: When temperature reaches between 500° C and 600° C some of the inclusions in the clay like carbon, sulfides and carbonates and salts are lost. The pots shrink by about 15% or more of their original mass at these temperatures.

claims.text: Pots are dried before firing so that steam from moisture left in the clay does not crack and break them.

quotes.quote: The pottery is dried before heat is applied to it to prevent the cracking and breakage of pots when the steam from excess moisture in the clay paste is released from the walls of the pot.

claims.text: Pots shrink while drying, and non-plastic inclusions reduce that shrinkage and keep the pottery from collapsing or warping.

quotes.quote: It is during this stage that the pots shrink and the non-plastic inclusions in the clay fabric reduce the shrinkage. The presence of non-plastic inclusions prevents the pottery from collapsing or warping.

claims.text: Large mineral inclusions in the clay paste raise a pot's thermal shock resistance, so it can survive the uneven, short firings of open fires.

quotes.quote: The large mineral inclusions in the clay paste increase the thermal shock resistance of the pot and thus can withstand the uneven and short firing episodes of open - fires

claims.text: Rapid cooling, like rapid heating, can crack or break pots and weakens the clay structure.

quotes.quote: Rapid cooling like rapid heating might result in breakage and cracking
Rapid heating and cooling weakens the clay structure and can make the pot less hard.

claims.text: Pots can be fired in open fires, small pits or bonfires, or in closed enclosures such as kilns and ovens.

quotes.quote: Pots can either be sun-dried or fired in open fires, in small pits or in bonfires, or in closed enclosures like kilns and ovens.

claims.text: In open firing, pots are placed directly on laid-out fuel and covered with more fuel, and uneven temperatures leave fireclouds or mottled colours.

quotes.quote: In open-firing, fuel is first laid out and the pots to be fired are placed directly on the fuel and are also covered with more fuel.
because the temperature is not uniform in all the places, it results in fireclouds or mottled colours on pottery

claims.text: Open fires reach low temperatures of 600° to 850° C, though fuels such as dung, ash and certain woods can take them over 900° C.

quotes.quote: The temperatures attained in open-fires are low and range between 600° and 850° C. The degree of temperature attained greatly depends on the fuel that is used. For instance fuels like dung, ash and certain types of wood when used can result in attaining temperatures of over 900° C

claims.text: D'source records a closed brick furnace at Sadum, and describes firing in the bhatti, an open circular furnace where ware is piled under coconut leaves and wood and covered with mud.

quotes.quote: The firing is done in the bhatti-traditional open furnace within a circular area. The articles are piled carefully and covered by locally available fuel such as dry coconut leaves, small wooden pieces. The kiln is covered with mud and fired to produce a very high temperature.
The closed furnace which isbuiltwith bricks is used to burn the finished products.

claims.text: Molela plaques are fired in the awara, a circular open brick kiln, loaded on cow dung cakes, sealed with potsherds and lit from openings at the bottom.

quotes.quote: The dried plaques are fired in a circular brick wood-fire kiln called awara, often shared by the community.

a circular open kiln, constructed from brick is one of the most convenient ways to fire the products in-house. The work is loaded into the bhatti on top of cowdung cakes and sealed with few layers of pottery shards.
Fire is lit from openings at the bottom of the kiln.

claims.text: D'source records that Molela firing reaches 600 to 700 degrees centigrade and lasts 4 to 6 hours.

quotes.quote: The firing temperature achieved is between 600 to 700 degrees centigrade. Firing lasts for 4 to 6 hours.

claims.text: Imp-art records Molela plaques fired at about 900o C for four hours, with artisans judging the temperature by the height of the flame.

quotes.quote: The plaques are fired at about 900o C for four hours, with the artisans visually estimating the temperature by the height of the flame, and maintaining it with a regular input of firewood and wood shavings.

claims.text: Jaipur blue pottery is fired in a traditional closed kiln of clay and brick, closed from above with wood fed from below.

quotes.quote: The final products are fired in a traditional closed kiln made out of clay and brick.
They are closed from above and wood is put from below.

claims.text: Jaipur blue pottery is fired at 800-850 degree Celsius.

quotes.quote: The temperature goes up to 800-850 degree Celsius.
Once the entire vessel is treated with the solution, the object is baked in a kiln at 800-850° C for six hours.

claims.text: In the Khemli terracotta cluster, ware dried for about a week is fired at around 700-1000 degree centigrade, where iron reacts with oxygen to give a reddish tone.

quotes.quote: Left again for drying, now for a week around, then fired in the kiln at around 700-1000 degree centigrade where the iron reacts with the oxygen to give it a natural reddish tone.

claims.text: At Villianur, firing gives the terracotta its characteristic reddish-brown colour and imparts strength.

quotes.quote: The firing process gives the terracotta its characteristic reddish- brown color and imparts strength.

claims.text: D'source describes Jaipur blue pottery as the only pottery technique that does not use clay.

quotes.quote: The distinguishing factor which makes the craft of Blue Pottery different from any other pottery techniques being practiced around the world is that it is the only pottery technique that does not use clay.

claims.text: Imp-art records the traditional blue glaze pottery body as ground quartz, glass, feldspar, and fuller's earth or kaolin clay, sieved and mixed with water.

quotes.quote: Traditionally, the moulding clay is made by passing ground quartz, glass, feldspar, and fuller's earth or kaolin clay through a sieve and adding water to form a fine paste.

claims.text: Blue pottery dough lacks plasticity, so large pieces break when pulled up on the wheel and are cast in plaster of Paris moulds instead.

quotes.quote: The dough used in blue pottery lacks plasticity due to which they can't be hard-pressed on wheel to make large products. The products break as the dough is pulled up. Therefore the products are casted in the molds.
Artisans develop molds in Plaster of Paris (POP) to caste the desired shape of the blue pottery products.

claims.text: In blue pottery, glass, a mixture of boric oxide and silica, lowers the firing temperature and helps in baking the quartz.

quotes.quote: Glass is basically a mixture of Boric Oxide and silica which reduces the temperature and also helps in baking the quartz.

claims.text: Blue pottery artisans have recently moved from the hand-driven chaak, or potter's wheel, to electric wheels, using the wheel for small pieces and vase necks.

quotes.quote: Chaak (Potter's Wheel): The artisans in recent years have started using electrical wheels instead of the traditional hand driven one. The potter's wheel is generally used to make small piece, necks of the vases or base or a product.

claims.text: Chunar's glaze is powdered glass mixed with clay, brushed on and fused to the unusual red clay in a second, high-temperature firing.

quotes.quote: what makes Chunar pottery unique is the application of glaze on a highly unusual red clay to give it a lustrous finish.

A glaze is then prepared by mixing powdered glass with clay and applied with the help of a brush. The pottery is further subjected to a second round of firing in a kiln at high temperatures, a critical process as it helps melt the glass and fuse it to the pottery.

claims.text: Khurja pottery uses a clay called safed mitti, or golden clay, mixed with quartz stone and feldspar procured from Gujarat and Rajasthan.

quotes.quote: A particular kind of clay called 'safed mitti' also known as golden clay, is used to prepare these pots. The other ingredients of this clay mix - quartz stone and feldspar- are procured from different states like Gujarat and Rajasthan.

claims.text: Khurja pieces are shaped by hand or electric machines, hand-painted with floral patterns, glazed and baked at high temperatures.

quotes.quote: The clay is then molded, either by hand or through electric machines, into various shapes like, pots, vases, tiles or items of crockery.
Each product is then smoothened and hand painted with intricate floral patterns in warm hues of earthy greens, reds, blues and browns.
The product is then glazed to add luster and ensure longevity and then baked at high temperatures fire to impart strength and highlight the colours.

claims.text: Pokhran pottery's light pink colour comes from a hard clay that is beaten, ground and sieved, unlike the normal red terracotta of other potters.

quotes.quote: Pokhran Pottery's light pink color is the result of a laborious process in which hard clay is beaten, ground and filtered through a sieve to get the appropriate fine texture. This clay has different properties than the normal red terracotta used by potters in the rest of the country.

claims.text: Villianur terracotta sculptures are built from coils or flattened slabs, dried, fired in a kiln and then embellished or painted with natural dyes.

quotes.quote: The sculptures are made using a coiled or slab construction method, where the clay is shaped into coils or flattened slabs and then assembled to form the desired shape.
Once firing is complete, the object is embellished or painted using natural dyes.

claims.text: At the Chhetra post-harvest festival, Rajwar women paint homes, niches, shelves and rice storage jars with lepai, a mixture of clay and cow dung.

quotes.quote: celebrate the post-harvest festival of Chhetra where the women paint homes and other items of daily use such as detha (niches), patani (shelves) and dodki (rice storage jars) with lepai, a mixture of clay and cow dung.

claims.text: Newer Molela imagery includes rural life, wedding processions and other secular themes, broadening the craft beyond seasonal ritual demand.

quotes.quote: More contemporary Molela imagery also includes scenes from rural life, wedding processions, and other secular themes that have broadened the appeal of the craft and provided artisans with more opportunities besides the seasonal demand for ritual plaques.

claims.text: Pokhran pottery is hand-painted with intricate floral or geometric patterns and then fired in a kiln to harden the clay and set the colours.

quotes.quote: Once dry, the clay products are hand- painted by the artisans. Intricate floral or geometric patterns are often found adorning these earthen pots and vases.
After the painting is complete these earthen wares are fired in a kiln at high temperatures in order to harden the clay and set the colors.

claims.text: Gorakhpur potters shape Kabis clay into bells, vases, animal figures, bullock carts and lamps, the horse being their most famous product.

quotes.quote: Skilled potters mold the 'Kabis' clay in to various shapes like bells, vases, animal figures, bullock carts and lamps.
Terracotta products, especially the famous horse, has caught the fancy of many over the years.

claims.text: Villianur terracotta works often depict scenes from Hindu mythology, local folklore and historical events.

quotes.quote: the Villianur Terracotta Works often depict scenes from Hindu mythology, local folklore and historical events.

claims.text: Longpi pottery is recognisable by its black colour and minimalist design, and traditionally comprised cookware.

quotes.quote: Recognisable through its characteristic black colour and minimalist design
Longpi pottery traditionally comprised cookware, but now also includes storage and serving vessels for food and beverages.

claims.text: Under KVIC's Kumhar Sashaktikaran Yojana, potter families in Nanded and Parbhani districts of Maharashtra received electric potter wheels after 10-day training.

quotes.quote: distributed electric potter wheels, through Video Conference, to 100 potter families in Nanded and Parbhani districts of Maharashtra as a major step ptowards empowerment with KumharSashaktikaranYojana of Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC)
who have been given 10-day training by KVIC.

claims.text: Minister Nitin Gadkari called KVIC's Kumhar Sashaktikaran Yojana the first initiative of its kind since independence to improve potters' lives.

quotes.quote: Shri Gadkari lauded the KumharSashaktikaranYojana of KVIC saying this was the first-of-its-kind initiative taken since independence to strengthen and improve the living of potters in the country.

claims.text: Molela artisans rely heavily on exhibitions, fairs and middlemen to sell their products, often resulting in low returns and inconsistent income.

quotes.quote: Besides the seasonal demand for their products, Molela artisans are heavily reliant on exhibitions, fairs and middlemen to sell their products, often resulting in low returns and inconsistent income

claims.text: Demand for Molela terracottas has declined significantly in recent years, and they face competition from cement and plaster imitations.

quotes.quote: the demand has also declined significantly in recent years. In particular, the terracottas face competition from cement and plaster imitations.

claims.text: For votive plaques, Molela artisans were traditionally paid in kind with grain or clothing, and they turn to agriculture in the lean months.

quotes.quote: For votive plaques, the artisans were traditionally paid in kind with items such as grains or clothing; they have historically practised agriculture during other times of the year to sustain themselves.
The craftspeople turn to agriculture to sustain themselves in the lean months.

claims.text: Demand for Molela plaques tends to be seasonal, as new vessels and votive murtis are needed at festival and harvest times.

quotes.quote: the demand for these plaques tends to be seasonal. New vessels and votive murtis are needed at festival and harvest times.

claims.text: Invest India's ODOP team trained 25 Molela terracotta artisans in design and packaging at a workshop on 30th September and 1st October 2021.

quotes.quote: This 'Craft and Design Workshop' organized by the ODOP Team at Invest India was a first-of-its-kind in which 4 design and packaging experts trained 25 inter-generational Molela Terracotta artisans with new design and packaging ideas on 30th September and 1st October 2021.

claims.text: Invest India's workshop gave Molela artisans ideas for diversifying into functional décor, planters and creeper tiles.

quotes.quote: This 2-day workshop resulted in training Molela Clay-Work artisans with fresh ideas for diversifying products across premium consumer demand product segments such as functional décor, planters, and creeper tiles.

claims.text: A DC(H)-sanctioned terracotta design project for 40 artisans developed 25 prototypes in a workshop at Khemli, Udaipur, from September 2015 to February 2016.

quotes.quote: sanctioned Integrated Design and Technical Development Project in Terracotta Craft for the 40 artisans to Export promotion council of Handicrafts, New Delhi.
During this 5 months workshop at khemli , Udaipur ,from 27th sept. 2015 - 26th Feb.2016, 25 prototypes with new designs were developed.

claims.text: An ORF commentary names Panchmura, Surul, Chaltaberia and Shetpur-Palpara as the major West Bengal villages exporting terracotta to international markets.

quotes.quote: Terracotta is still of high interest in the global market where Panchmura, Surul, Chaltaberia and Shetpur-Palpara are the major villages in West Bengal that exports terracotta to international markets.

claims.text: An ORF commentary on Bankura's terracotta lists equipment and transport problems, little contact with Kolkata buyers, reliance on local patronage, scarce capital and falling demand as problems its artisans face.

quotes.quote: the issues of equipment, transportation and other logistical problems; the lack of interaction between the artisans and the urban consumers in Kolkata; the terracotta artisans are mostly dependent on local patronage;
the inadequate capital, sluggish marketing and falling demand are causing these marginalized artisans to become extinct
However, the artisans face some key problems that are crippling the market for this kind of artwork

claims.text: A Panchmura potter told an ORF author that many local youngsters, his son among them, have moved to Kolkata rather than take up the laborious craft.

quotes.quote: He woefully adds that a large number of youngsters in the area, including his own son, have moved to Kolkata not only because of the money but also their inability to commit to the labour required for this kind of artistry.

claims.text: A study of women potters in Tuichindrai village, Khowai, Tripura, found they make clay idols of Hindu gods and earn their biggest profits from idols.

quotes.quote: A study was conducted with 12 female potters from the Tuichindrai village in the Teliamura block of Khowai Tripura.
People in Tuichindrai create various pots and vessels, as also clay idols of Hindu gods and goddesses, decorative items, and ritual artifacts. They make their biggest profits by selling idols.

claims.text: An IIM Bangalore fellow names lack of raw materials, high-quality goods from outside potters and low income from wholesalers as main difficulties for the Tuichindrai potters of Khowai, Tripura.

quotes.quote: Lack of raw materials, the availability of high-quality goods made by outside potters in the local markets, and low income from wholesalers are some of the main difficulties the pottery community is currently facing.
A study was conducted with 12 female potters from the Tuichindrai village in the Teliamura block of Khowai Tripura.

claims.text: An IIM Bangalore fellow cites a 2021 study by Jahanara and others in which only 10% of potters relied solely on pottery, low profit having driven them to other work.

quotes.quote: According to a study by Jahanara et al., 2021, it was found that due to low profit, potters changed their line of work. Only 10% of them relied solely on pottery because it could do not provide for their basic needs.

claims.text: Mathew Sasa Craft, started in Delhi in 2007, and the Ministry of Minority Affairs' USTTAD scheme of September 2015 work to preserve Longpi pottery.

quotes.quote: At present, initiatives like Mathew Sasa Craft, started by Longpi craftsperson Mathew Sasa in Delhi in 2007, and USTTAD (Upgrading the Skills and Training in Traditional Arts/Crafts for Development) started by the Ministry of Minority Affairs in September 2015, are working to preserve the craft

claims.text: NID's USTTAD project for Manipur black pottery began with a 15-day field visit and developed planters, furniture, cookware, serveware and table accessories.

quotes.quote: The project was initiated with a 15-day field visit to Manipur
The product category broadly includes planters, furniture, cookware, serveware, and table accessories.

claims.text: Bankura district's terracotta crafts are mainly concentrated in Bishnupur and in the village of Panchmura.

quotes.quote: These beautiful artworks are mainly concentrated in Bishnupur and Panchmura of Bankura District.
Take a tour to Panchmura village which is the home to famous terracotta industry.

claims.text: Panchmura village near Bishnupur, in Bankura district, is one of the main hubs of terracotta in West Bengal.

quotes.quote: Panchmura village near Bishnupur, Bankura District is one of the main hubs of terracotta in West Bengal.

claims.text: An ORF commentary attributes Bengal terracotta to the lack of stone and the alluvial soil left by the Damodar, Dwarakeshwar and Kangsabati rivers in Bankura.

quotes.quote: Terracotta came into existence in Bengal due to the unavailability of stones and large endowments of alluvial soil left by the main rivers in the Bankura district: Damodar, Dwarakeshwar and the Kangsabati.

claims.text: A Panchmura artisan says Bankura's soil is denser and more mineral-rich than Kolkata's, making a Bankura Durga idol at least thrice as heavy.

quotes.quote: A Panchmura artisan says that a Durga idol made in Bankura is at least thrice as heavy as an idol of the same size made in Kolkata because the soil found in Bankura is much denser and mineral-rich, making the crafting process extremely laborious.

claims.text: A DC(H) project report calls Molela, a village in Rajsamand district, the traditional home of Rajasthani terracotta art.

claims.text: Nizamabad in Azamgarh district is known for its black pottery.

quotes.quote: Nizamabad-Azamgarh is known for its Black Pottery.

claims.text: Jaipur city has historically been the main centre for producing blue pottery, which later spread in small pockets around Jaipur.
