claims.text: Workshops making wares similar to Jaipur's blue glaze pottery have appeared in regions such as Chinhat near Lucknow in Uttar Pradesh.

quotes.quote: several other workshops producing similar wares have cropped up in regions such as Chinhat near Lucknow in present-day Uttar Pradesh.

claims.text: Longpi pottery, locally ham or hampai, is named after the Longpi villages of Ukhrul district, Manipur, which yield its material.

the village of Longpi, located in Ukhrul district at Manipur has been identified as a key cluster where several Christians actively practice the craft of black pottery.

The practice of terracotta craft has been happening for many generations.

quotes.quote: The Villianur Terrracotta works are handicrafts popular in the Villianur region of Puducherry.

quotes.quote: The Pokhran region, with its abundant clay deposits and skilled artisans, has been a centre for pottery production for a very long time.

lede.text: Terracotta means 'baked earth' and has been used for decorative art works and building construction since ancient times; its clay is a fine-grained material that is plastic with water and hardens when dried or fired.

The category joins terracotta and pottery works, thrown on the wheel or built by hand and fired red, black or glazed, with other mud-based crafts: Molela's hollow-relief votive plaques, Melaghar's pressed clay work and Lucknow's carved and painted clay figures.
It is made by communities such as the Kumhar caste at Molela, the Kummari at Sadum, the Karmakar of Khowai, Tangkhul Naga men at Longpi and the Kumbhars of Lucknow's Prajapati community.

Its record runs from the chaff-tempered ceramics of Mehrgarh and the painted red pottery of the Indus, through Black and Red Ware and Northern Black Polished Ware, to centres such as Khurja, Chunar and Molela.

sentences.text: The term pottery refers to low-fired, unvitrified objects and ceramic to high-fired, vitrified wares, a word derived from the Greek keramos, meaning burned material or earthenware.
Terracotta figures of deities have a ritual role in India, and the V&A calls the Bankura clay horse the most well-known type of ritual pottery from India.

Votive terracotta is made by members of the Hindu potter caste, such as the Kumhars, whose name comes from the Sanskrit kumbhakar, earthen pot-maker, while its customer is often from a tribal community.
At Sadum the men normally throw on the wheel and the women decorate, while at Longpi the craft is traditionally a domain of men, though women are not barred from it.
Clay figure modelling has been widely practised in India for hundreds of years, for worship, as toys, as ornament and for ethnographic purposes.
Lucknow is famous for its clay toys, crafted by Kumbhars of the Prajapati community in sets of figurines and fruits.
Rajwar clay art of Chhattisgarh, a decorative relief clay art popularised by Sonabai Rajwar, has three aspects: lepai, jhinjhari kala or jaali work, and pakha lekha or relief work.
Pottery was the first synthetic material made by humans, and the earliest ceramics of the subcontinent, from Period IB at Mehrgarh, are handmade, buff, chaff-tempered and soft.
Mehrgarh's Period IIA pottery shows slab forming, and its Period IIB pottery was wheel-turned and shaped by the paddle and anvil method.
Indus potters made wheel-made red pottery painted with black motifs, though painted pottery was less than 10% of the whole, the rest being unpainted and used every day.
The most common Indus kiln is the updraft type, and Mound E at Harappa, one of its oldest mounds, has pottery kilns beside workshops for agate, shell and copper goods.
Other wares include Ochre Coloured Pottery, the post-Harappan Painted Grey Ware largely dated to 1100-400 BCE, and the glossy Northern Black Polished Ware dated to between 700 BCE and 200 BCE.
Black and Red Ware, first described by Mortimer Wheeler in 1947, spans the Neolithic to the Early Historic Period across most of the subcontinent.

Nearly three-quarters of Indus terracotta animal figurines represent cattle, and the V&A records Bankura clay horses, elephants and tigers bought by villagers as offerings to the forest gods, a ritual offering no longer widespread.

Khurja is said to have been established as a ceramic centre in the 14th century, Chunar glaze pottery traces its origin to the 17th century, and in the 18th century naturalistic clay models were centred in Krishnanagar, Lucknow and Poona.
Ceramics have three basic raw materials: clay, a fine-grained material that is plastic at appropriate water contents and hardens when dried or fired, non-plastic inclusions, and water.
The major clay mineral groups are kaolinite, smectite or montmorillonite, and illite.
Kaolinites have large particles and fire to white or yellow, smectites have very small particles and are very plastic with high shrinkage, and illites have small particles and good plasticity.
Common clays, which often contain illite and smectite mixed-layer minerals, serve ceramics in general, while fuller's earth, sold as Multani Mitti, is mainly montmorillonite.
Potters add non-plastic inclusions, from ash, husk and chaff to quartz, lime and grog, making up 20% to 50% of the total volume.

At Molela the potters mix nada, a coarse black clay with a high sand grog, and the finer grey alu, but sources differ on the dung: D'source records 20% dried donkey dung, Incredible India sifted cow dung.
Longpi pottery is made of powdered black serpentine rock, mixed with clay in NID's account and with a weathered reddish-brown rock in Imp-art's.

Sources differ on whether Jaipur blue pottery's quartz and glass body contains clay: D'source calls it the only pottery technique that does not use clay, while Imp-art lists fuller's earth or kaolin clay in it.
Most clay minerals are layered silicates, built of tetrahedral and octahedral sheets in 1:1 layers about 0.7 nm thick or 2:1 layers about 1 nm thick.

Pottery needs a minimum of 550°C for considerable hardness and durability; one source places the onset of sintering at 585° C for kaolinite and 678° C for smectite, while a ceramics review puts sintering above 800°C.
Oxidising firing burns off organic matter to give a light colour, while in reducing conditions carbon from the fuels is deposited on the pots, leaving black or dark brown surfaces.
At Sadum ware comes out red when smoke escapes through the kiln vents and black when the vents are fully covered, and Nizamabad's black colour comes from keeping the kiln airtight.
In the Khemli cluster, ware fired at around 700-1000 degree centigrade turns reddish as iron reacts with oxygen, and the red ochre slip of Indus pots turned bright red in the kiln.
Glazes consist of silica, fluxes that lower their melting point and metallic oxides that give colour, and Chunar fuses a glaze of powdered glass and clay to its red clay in a second firing.
In Jaipur blue pottery, glass, a mixture of boric oxide and silica, lowers the firing temperature, and the ware is fired at 800-850 degree Celsius.
Between 500° C and 600° C a pot loses some inclusions such as carbon, sulfides, carbonates and salts, and at 900° C clay minerals lose their structure and form new silicate minerals.
Plasticity lets a material be deformed under stress without rupturing and keep its new shape, and bentonites are the most plastic of the common clays.
Ball clays crack when dried, bentonites can take a week to dry and kaolins dry quickly with little shrinkage, while large amounts of smectite may develop undesirable shrinkage.
Non-plastic inclusions reduce shrinkage and keep pots from collapsing or warping as they dry, and large mineral inclusions raise thermal shock resistance for uneven open firings.
Pots are dried before firing so that steam does not crack them, and rapid heating or cooling can crack them and weaken the clay structure.
Molela figures are built hollow so that heat spreads evenly and cracking is minimised, and D'source and Imp-art say the donkey dung in their clay disperses heat during firing.
Open fires reach 600° to 850° C, and Harappan updraft kilns sent heat through platform vents partly covered with potsherds so that it would not break the pottery.
Paddle and anvil beating makes the pot wall thin and compact, increasing its strength and decreasing its porosity.
Blue pottery dough lacks plasticity, so large pieces are cast in plaster of Paris moulds rather than pulled up on the wheel.
Clay is cleaned by hand-picking or by pounding and sieving dried clay, in more recent times very fine clay is separated by levigation, and the clay is kneaded to remove air pockets.
Pots are formed by hand-building, through pinching, slab building, moulds and coiling, the most common hand technique, or by throwing on the wheel.
In the paddle and anvil method a stone anvil is held inside a leather-hard pot while a wooden paddle beats the outside, like the raayi and salapa of Sadum and the hamkapi of Longpi.
Slipping coats the pot with liquid clay before firing, and burnishing with a stone or smoothed potsherd reduces porosity by aligning the clay particles on the surface.
Pots are fired in open fires, small pits, bonfires or kilns, and in open firing they sit directly on the fuel, where uneven temperatures leave fireclouds or mottled colours.

D'source records both a closed brick furnace and firing in the bhatti, an open circular furnace covered with mud, at Sadum, while Molela potters fire in the awara, a circular brick kiln loaded over cow dung cakes.
Sources differ on Molela firing, one recording 600 to 700 degrees centigrade for 4 to 6 hours and another about 900 degrees C for four hours.
Melaghar and Palpada's pressed clay work is press formed inside plaster-of-Paris moulds, while Lucknow clay figures are tooled and carved in a green stage and then painted.
Clays are products of the weathering of silicate rocks, composed mainly of silica and alumina, and their formation is a chemical process assisted by mechanical breakdown.

Primary clays stay at their parent rock and are coarse and non-plastic, while secondary clays, transported by streams, rivers, glaciation, erosion and wind, are more common, finer and more homogenous.
Kaolinites form through intense weathering and acid leaching, smectites are characteristic of arid and alkaline environments, and bentonite forms through the weathering of volcanic glass.
Longpi sits on serpentine rock that its villagers dig from a nearby hill, and an ORF commentary ties Bengal terracotta to the lack of stone and the alluvial soil left by Bankura's rivers.
Molela's clay is typically collected during the monsoon, when it is most abundant, and moulding is done in the monsoon because humidity in the air helps reduce cracking.
The men of Longpi dig serpentine rock between September and March so that it can be used through the long monsoon months.

In Panchmura the potter's wheel stops in the holy time of Baisakh, in April and May, believed to be when Lord Shiva appears from the wheel, though many also cite heat that tires artisans and cracks pottery.
Bankura district's terracotta is mainly concentrated in Bishnupur and Panchmura, one of the main hubs of terracotta in West Bengal.
Nizamabad in Azamgarh district is known for black pottery, and Gorakhpur terracotta is practised by families of the villages of Aurangabad, Gularia, Bharwalia and Budhadih.

A DC(H) project report calls Molela in Rajsamand district the traditional home of Rajasthani terracotta art, while Jaipur city has been the main centre for producing blue pottery and the Pokhran region, with abundant clay deposits, a centre for pottery production for a very long time.

Villianur terracotta is popular in the Villianur region of Puducherry, Sadum in Chittoor district has practised terracotta for many generations, and Longpi pottery is named after the Longpi villages of Ukhrul district, Manipur.
Arnold is of the opinion that potters obtain clay 1 to 6 kilometers from the manufacturing site, and Imp-art places Molela's alu clay in the bed of the nearby Banas River and local ponds.
Workshops making wares similar to Jaipur's blue glaze pottery have appeared in regions such as Chinhat near Lucknow in Uttar Pradesh.

Melaghar and Palpada villages of West Tripura district are known for pressed clay work, and GI applicants include pottery societies at Manamadurai in Sivaganga, Tyrshang in West Jaintia Hills and Chunar in Mirzapur.
Demand for Molela plaques is seasonal, at festival and harvest times, and its artisans were traditionally paid in kind and turn to agriculture in the lean months.
Molela artisans rely on exhibitions, fairs and middlemen, with low returns and inconsistent income, and face competition from cement and plaster imitations.

An ORF commentary on Bankura's terracotta lists equipment and transport problems, reliance on local patronage, scarce capital and falling demand, and a Panchmura potter told ORF that many local youngsters, his son among them, have moved to Kolkata.

An IIM Bangalore fellow cites a 2021 study in which only 10% of potters relied solely on pottery, but found pottery the only livelihood for 91.6 percent of the women potters studied in Tuichindrai, Tripura, who face lack of raw materials and low income from wholesalers.
Under KVIC's Kumhar Sashaktikaran Yojana, potter families in Nanded and Parbhani districts received electric potter wheels after 10-day training.
A DC(H)-sanctioned project for 40 artisans at Khemli, Udaipur, developed 25 prototypes between September 2015 and February 2016, and Invest India trained 25 Molela artisans in 2021.

The V&A records the Bankura horse as the motif of the Central Cottage Industries Emporium and INTACH as the official crest motif of the All India Handicrafts Board, and ORF names Panchmura among West Bengal's major terracotta-exporting villages.

The GI registry lists Blue Pottery of Jaipur and Molela Clay Work among registrations of April 2008 to March 2009 and the Asharikandi and Lyrnai crafts among those of April 2023 to March 2024, though Imp-art says Molela's GI appears to have brought artisans little benefit.
Classical Harappan pottery is mostly reddish pink or buff, painted black on red or dark brown on buff, while most Black and Red Ware has a red exterior and a black interior.
Chandraketugarh terracottas are known for a unique visual style, often embellished with distinctive surface stippling.
The Bankura district page says the long-necked Bankura horse comes in seven separate parts that are assembled, and a c.1944 example in the V&A is hollow with applied pellet eyes.
Molela plaques show Hindu deities, regional divinities and folk heroes, and newer imagery adds rural life, wedding processions and other secular themes.

Khurja originally produced pottery with slip decoration raised in slight relief, white and blue on an orange-brown or claret ground, and Pokhran pottery is hand-painted with intricate floral or geometric patterns.
At Nizamabad women etch intricate patterns on the dried clay with a fine needle, and Longpi pottery is recognisable by its black colour and minimalist design.
Rajwar clay art, made mainly of bamboo and clay by women adorning walls and doors, shows geometric shapes and motifs inspired by nature.

Lucknow potters were renowned for fruit and vegetable models said to be so lifelike they defied detection unless handled, and in the early 19th century a red ochre coating likened their figures to Italian terracottas.
